---
title: "Turning a question into a comparison"
---

Suppose we want to know whether an aspectual mismatch makes a sentence harder to process. We design two conditions and observe the following average reading times at a critical verb:

| condition | average reading time |
|---|---:|
| aspectually matched | 410 ms |
| aspectually mismatched | 455 ms |

The mismatch condition is 45 ms slower. What does that difference tell us?

By itself, not very much. Perhaps mismatch caused additional processing. Perhaps the mismatch sentences contained less frequent verbs. Perhaps a small number of participants produced the difference. The subtraction is correct, but its linguistic interpretation depends on how the observations and comparison were constructed.

We will work from the research question to the numerical comparison one step at a time.

## Step 1: identify the response

The [**response**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms) is the measurement whose variation we want to understand. In this experiment, it might be reading time at the critical verb.

We need to say more than “reading time.” Is the measurement the first-pass time, total time, or time from a particular reading procedure? Is it recorded in milliseconds or transformed before analysis? Which region supplies it?

A precise statement is:

> The response is the total reading time in milliseconds at the critical verb on one participant and sentence trial.

This sentence also identifies the unit of analysis.

## Step 2: identify the linguistic contrast

The main [**predictor**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms) distinguishes the observations that the theory says should differ. Here it records whether a trial contains an aspectually matched or mismatched context.

The values must correspond to an actual design contrast. If all matched sentences contain one set of verbs and all mismatched sentences contain another, the predictor does not isolate aspectual mismatch. It also separates the two verb sets.

This is why theoretically interesting predictors are more than available columns. Their values should encode a linguistic distinction for which an account predicts a change in the response.

For a dative-choice study, predictors might encode whether the recipient is pronominal, whether the theme is discourse-new, and how the lengths of the two arguments compare. These variables express proposals about accessibility, information structure, and production difficulty. Trial number or recording channel may also matter, but for a different reason: they describe the design or measurement process.

## Step 3: say which observations are being compared

Imagine that every participant sees both conditions and every sentence appears in both conditions across participants. The comparison then occurs within participants and within sentence items.

This structure matters. A comparison between different groups of participants may reflect preexisting group differences. A comparison between different item sets may reflect lexical differences. A within-participant and within-item design rules out some of these alternative descriptions by construction.

We can now expand the analysis statement:

> The response is total reading time at the critical verb on one participant and sentence trial. The comparison is between aspectually matched and mismatched trials, with both conditions represented within participants and sentence items.

## Step 4: state the estimand

The [**estimand**](https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9-R1_Step4_Guideline_2019_1203.pdf) is the population quantity we want to learn about. Let $\mu_{\mathrm{mismatch}}$ be the mean reading time for mismatch trials in the target population, and let $\mu_{\mathrm{match}}$ be the corresponding mean for match trials. One possible estimand is

$$
\tau
=\mu_{\mathrm{mismatch}}
-\mu_{\mathrm{match}}.
$$

In words, $\tau$ is the difference in mean reading time between the mismatch and match conditions.

The population still needs to be specified. Do we mean only these participants and sentences, or new readers and new sentence items from populations represented by the experiment? The design must contain the relevant replication if the broader target is to be plausible.

Our complete statement is now:

> One observation is a participant's reading of the critical verb in one sentence. The response is total reading time in milliseconds. The comparison is the within-participant and within-item contrast between aspectually matched and mismatched contexts. The target is the difference in mean reading time for readers and items from the populations represented by the design.

Writing this statement takes only a few sentences. It prevents the fitted coefficient from acquiring a broader interpretation than the data and design support.

## The same records can answer a different question

Suppose the experiment also asks participants to choose an interpretation after each sentence. We can now ask at least three questions:

1. Does mismatch change reading time?
2. Does mismatch change the probability of choosing one interpretation?
3. Do participants with larger reading-time differences also show larger interpretation differences?

These questions use overlapping records, but their responses and estimands differ. The first has a time response. The second has a categorical response. The third compares participant-level contrasts.

Thus a dataset does not come with one inevitable analysis. The research question determines which observations, response, comparison, and target are relevant.

## What can go wrong?

### The unit does not match the claim

Suppose a corpus contains thousands of tokens from one speaker. Those data may describe that speaker's production precisely. They do not show how speakers vary because only one speaker was observed.

### The predictor does not isolate the contrast

Suppose every mismatch sentence uses one set of verbs and every match sentence uses another. The condition difference combines mismatch and lexical identity. Collecting more observations will estimate that combined difference more precisely, but it will not separate the two sources.

### The evaluation answers a different question

Suppose a model is meant to predict responses for new readers, but its training and test sets contain trials from the same readers. The evaluation measures prediction of additional trials from observed readers. It does not measure transfer to new readers.

These problems arise before the choice of estimator. A more elaborate model cannot recover a comparison that the data never contained.

## Exploration can change the question

Exploratory analysis may show that the original target was poorly chosen. A slider response, for instance, may contain many observations at both endpoints. A target concerned only with average slider position may miss a theoretically important distinction between endpoint and interior responses.

The right response is to write a revised question and target. Exploration is allowed to change the analysis. The change should be explicit so that the new result is not presented as if it answered the original question unchanged.

## Test the distinction

1. A corpus study asks whether discourse-new themes favor the prepositional dative. State the unit, response, predictor, comparison, and target.
2. A study averages acceptability judgments by sentence before analysis but interprets its result as variation among participants. Which variation has already been removed?
3. A word-recognition model is evaluated by randomly splitting trials, but the intended target is performance on new word types. How should the split change?
